passages.text: Few behaviors are as Ⓐ<u>resistant</u> to suggestion as yawning: merely seeing, hearing, or even reading about someone else's yawn can elicit one of our own. Scientists still do not fully comprehend why yawns are contagious. One theory ascribes the effect to empathy, noting that people are prone to catch yawns more readily from family members and friends than from Ⓑ<u>strangers</u>. Young children rarely catch yawns before the age of about four, around the time they begin to Ⓒ<u>grasp</u> what other people are thinking and feeling. Other researchers are Ⓓ<u>skeptical</u> of the empathy explanation, pointing out that the link diminishes once age and attention are taken into account. As for why we yawn at all, one hypothesis is that yawning helps Ⓔ<u>cool</u> the brain, since it draws in a large breath of air and enhances blood flow to the head. Whatever its purpose, the yawn remains a small enigma that virtually everyone has experienced.

Most substances become denser as they cool and freeze, so their solid form sinks in their own liquid. Water is a conspicuous Ⓐ<u>exception</u>. As it freezes, its molecules lock into an open, hexagonal arrangement that occupies more space than liquid water, so ice is less dense and Ⓑ<u>floats</u>. This peculiar property has prodigious consequences for life. When a lake freezes in winter, the ice forms at the surface and acts as a Ⓒ<u>conductor</u>, retarding the loss of heat from the water beneath it. Fish and other organisms can therefore Ⓓ<u>survive</u> the winter in the liquid water below. If ice sank, lakes in cold regions might freeze from the bottom up and remain Ⓔ<u>frozen</u> for much of the year. The same expansion explains why water pipes can rupture in winter and why rocks fracture when water seeps into them and freezes.

Teachers have long quipped that the best way to learn something is to teach it, and research suggests that the jest contains genuine truth. Ⓐ In several experiments, students who studied material expecting to explain it to others later retained it better than students who expected only to take a test on it. Ⓑ Preparing to teach seems to compel learners to organize information, discern the main ideas, and anticipate questions. Ⓒ Actually articulating the material adds further benefits, because gaps in understanding become evident the moment a learner tries to put an idea into words. Ⓓ Many universities now record their lectures and post them online so that students can watch them at any time. Ⓔ Researchers sometimes call this the protégé effect, and some schools put it to use by having older pupils tutor younger ones. Even explaining a lesson to an imaginary listener appears to be beneficial.

Space debris, the burgeoning cloud of junk that humanity has left in orbit since the first satellite was launched in 1957, poses an escalating menace to spacecraft. ( Ⓐ ) It includes dead satellites, spent rocket stages, and innumerable fragments from explosions and collisions, all traveling at several kilometers per second. ( Ⓑ ) At such speeds, even a fragment the size of a coin can cripple a functioning spacecraft, and the International Space Station routinely adjusts its orbit to evade passing debris. ( Ⓒ ) The problem has intensified substantially in recent years as companies have launched thousands of small satellites to furnish internet service from space; one company alone had placed more than six thousand in orbit by 2025. ( Ⓓ ) As early as 1978, Donald Kessler, a researcher at NASA, predicted that, beyond a certain density of objects, each collision would produce fragments that cause still more collisions, a chain reaction that could render some orbits unusable for generations. ( Ⓔ ) To avert this, regulators now oblige operators to remove satellites from orbit within a few years after their missions end, and several companies are testing spacecraft designed to retrieve derelict satellites.

In the tragedies of ancient Athens, a group of performers called the chorus stood between the actors and the audience. Its members sang and danced, remarked on the action, and articulated the anxieties and aspirations of ordinary citizens, but over time the chorus's role Ⓐ[expanded / diminished]. Aeschylus, the earliest of the great tragedians, gave it long and central passages, but in the plays of Euripides, written a generation or two later, its songs often seem only loosely connected to the plot. Some scholars attribute this decline to the burgeoning importance of individual actors, whose number had Ⓑ[increased / decreased] from one to three. Marketers have long known that adding an option nobody wants can alter what people choose. In one renowned classroom demonstration, a periodical offered three subscriptions: online only for $59, print only for $125, and print plus online for the same $125. Almost no one chose the print-only option, yet its presence mattered: when students saw all three offers, most gravitated toward the combined subscription; when the print-only option was removed, many more opted for the cheaper online version instead. The superfluous option served as a decoy, making the combined package look like a bargain by comparison. Psychologists call this the decoy effect, and it manifests itself in many settings, from restaurant menus that list one exorbitantly priced wine to cinemas that price a medium popcorn only marginally below the large.

The Venus flytrap is one of the few plants that move quickly enough for people to watch. Each trap consists of two hinged lobes lined with minuscule trigger hairs. If an insect touches one hair, nothing happens; but if it touches a second hair, or the same hair again, within about twenty seconds, the trap snaps shut in a fraction of a second. This counting system prevents the plant from squandering energy on raindrops or falling debris. Once closed, the trap seals itself hermetically and secretes digestive juices, and it may take a week or more to assimilate the insect's nutrients. Although the plant is sold worldwide, it grows wild only in a confined area of wetlands in North and South Carolina in the United States.

The jigsaw classroom, a teaching method devised by the social psychologist Elliot Aronson, was designed to replace competition among students with cooperation. Aronson developed it in 1971 in Austin, Texas, where schools had only lately been desegregated and tension between students of different backgrounds was acute. He discerned that ordinary classrooms fostered competition: students raised their hands avidly, hoping the teacher would call on them rather than on a classmate. In his alternative, students were divided into small, mixed groups, and each member was given one segment of a lesson, such as one period of a renowned person's life. To learn the whole lesson, students had to listen attentively to one another. Within weeks, observers reported less hostility and more goodwill among classmates, and students' test scores held steady or rose.

Barcelona's superblocks, including a pioneering one that opened in the Poblenou district in 2016, have become a test of how far cities can go in taking streets back from cars. Shopkeepers dreaded losing passing trade, and residents of nearby avenues lamented traffic Ⓑ<u>pushing</u> onto their streets by the closures. Inside the zone, the few vehicles still allowed in were held to about ten kilometers per hour, and parking spaces gave way to trees and picnic tables. Later studies reported less noise inside such zones, although some found that rents nearby had risen as the area grew more desirable. The city went on to create more superblocks, Ⓒ<u>making</u> Barcelona a model for planners across Europe. The James Webb Space Telescope, which began scientific operations in 2022, has Ⓐ<u>surprised</u> astronomers by challenging orthodox ideas about how the first galaxies formed. These observations have drawn attention far beyond the scientific community. Because light takes time to travel, looking at distant objects means looking back in time, and Webb's large mirror and sensitivity to infrared light allow it to observe galaxies as they were when the universe was very young. Prevailing theories of cosmic history predicted that these early galaxies would be small and Ⓑ<u>faint</u>, since there had been little time for stars to form. Instead, Webb has found a number that appear unexpectedly bright and massive, including one, reported in 2024, whose light left it less than 300 million years after the Big Bang. Some researchers conjecture that early stars formed more Ⓒ<u>slowly</u> than expected; others speculate that growing black holes may make certain galaxies appear more luminous than they really are. The findings do not Ⓓ<u>overturn</u> the Big Bang itself, as some sensational headlines proclaimed, but they are compelling scientists to Ⓔ<u>revise</u> their models of how the first galaxies evolved.

Breaking, often called breakdancing, shows what a street culture gains and risks when it becomes an Olympic sport. For decades it remained an Ⓐ<u>official</u> art form, transmitted in streets, clubs, and community centers rather than in academies. Advocates anticipated that the Olympic stage would bring the dance new Ⓑ<u>recognition</u> and funding, and the competitions drew vast, rapturous crowds. The first gold medals went to dancers from Japan and Canada, yet the debut also exposed Ⓒ<u>tensions</u>. Whatever its Olympic future, breaking continues to Ⓔ<u>thrive</u> in battles around the world.

Daylight saving time, the practice of moving clocks an hour forward or back twice a year, is now widely disputed. At the same time, the energy savings that originally Ⓓ<u>justified</u> the practice now appear to be negligible, since modern households use electricity for heating, cooling, and screens at all hours. ____, the European Parliament voted in 2019 to end seasonal clock changes, but member states could not agree on whether to keep summer or winter time permanently, and the plan languished. People often discern faces where none exist: in the front of a car, in a cloud, or in the burn marks on a slice of toast. Black bears survive northern winters by entering a state of dormancy that can last five months or more. During this period their heart rate plummets, although their body temperature falls by only a few degrees, and they neither eat, drink, nor Ⓐ<u>urinate</u>. How long a teacher waits after asking a question can profoundly affect the quality of students' answers, as the science educator Mary Budd Rowe discovered in the early 1970s. Ⓐ After posing a question, most teachers waited less than a second before answering it themselves, reiterating it, or calling on another student. Ⓑ Rowe speculated about what would happen if teachers simply paused for three seconds or more. Ⓒ In classrooms where teachers learned to wait, students gave more elaborate answers, offered more evidence for their claims, and were less likely to say that they did not know. Ⓓ Science classrooms of that period were often equipped with new laboratory furniture paid for by government programs. Ⓔ Reticent students, who need more time to organize their thoughts, also began to take part more often. The finding implies that a few seconds of silence, though it may feel disconcerting, is one of the cheapest teaching tools available.

Across much of Asia, Europe, and North America, pets are increasingly treated as members of the family. ( Ⓐ ) Owners now procure organic food, health insurance, and even strollers for their animals, and spending on pet products and services has burgeoned into a global industry worth hundreds of billions of dollars. ( Ⓑ ) South Korea offers a striking example of how quickly attitudes toward animals can evolve. ( Ⓒ ) Yet in January 2024, its National Assembly passed a law banning the breeding and slaughter of dogs for meat, with the ban due to take full effect in 2027. ( Ⓓ ) Farmers who had raised dogs for decades were offered compensation to shutter their businesses. ( Ⓔ ) Still, the rise of the pet economy poses new dilemmas, from the welfare of animals bred for fashionable looks to the number of pets forsaken when their owners lose interest.

The calendar now used in most countries grew out of a sixteenth-century correction to an ancient error. The earlier calendar, introduced by Julius Caesar, presupposed that a year lasts exactly 365.25 days. The true solar year is about eleven minutes shorter, a minuscule error that nonetheless Ⓐ[accumulated / disappeared] over the centuries. By the sixteenth century, the calendar had drifted some ten days away from the seasons, which perturbed church officials who computed the date of Easter. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII decreed a correction: ten days were simply dropped, so that in Catholic countries Thursday, October 4, was followed by Friday, October 15. The reform was accepted Ⓑ[quickly / reluctantly] in Catholic lands, but many Protestant and Orthodox countries, wary of a decree from Rome, resisted for generations. People often work less hard in a group than they do alone, a tendency that was first measured more than a century ago. In the early twentieth century, the French agricultural engineer Maximilien Ringelmann had volunteers tug on a rope, sometimes individually and sometimes in teams, and recorded how hard they pulled. To his astonishment, the total force of a group was considerably less than the sum of what its members could pull individually, and the shortfall widened as groups became larger. Later researchers replicated the same pattern when people were asked to clap or shout as loudly as possible. Part of the loss comes from poor coordination, but much of it reflects reduced effort: when individual contributions cannot be identified, people are inclined to exert less effort. Psychologists call this social loafing, and it diminishes when each member's contribution is visible, when the task feels meaningful, and when groups are small.

Caffeine is the most widely consumed stimulant in the world, and its effect depends on an ingenious deception. Throughout the day, a chemical called adenosine accumulates in the brain and binds to receptors that make us feel drowsy. Caffeine molecules are similar enough in shape to fit those receptors, blocking adenosine without activating them, so the signal of tiredness is muffled. The effect does not persist forever: in a typical adult, the amount of caffeine in the blood falls by half in roughly five hours, although this varies widely between individuals. Regular drinkers also develop tolerance, as the brain responds by generating more receptors, which is why heavy coffee drinkers often feel lethargic and irritable when they abruptly stop.

The Pomodoro Technique is a time-management method that divides work into short, timed intervals separated by brief breaks. It was devised in the late 1980s by Francesco Cirillo, a university student in Italy who, frustrated by his inability to concentrate, began timing his study sessions with a kitchen timer shaped like a tomato. He would work on a single task until the timer rang after twenty-five minutes, then take a short break of about five minutes. After four such sessions, he permitted himself a lengthier respite; the name of the method comes from the Italian word for tomato. Its appeal lies partly in its simplicity: a fixed, short interval makes large tasks feel less daunting, and regular breaks alleviate mental fatigue. Research on the technique itself is sparse, but studies of breaks and attention lend some credence to its fundamental premise.

Heat waves are not confined to land: marine heatwaves, periods in which ocean temperatures remain anomalously high for days or months, have become more frequent and more intense as the climate warms. Legal sports betting has spread rapidly across the United States since 2018, when the Supreme Court struck down a federal law that had largely confined it to Nevada. Many European languages require speakers to choose between two forms of "you." French distinguishes tu from vous, German du from Sie, and Spanish tú from usted. Korean and Japanese, which mark respect through verb endings and distinctive vocabulary, take the notion even further. Linguists call this the T–V distinction, after the Latin pronouns tu and vos. Traditionally, the choice Ⓐ<u>concealed</u> social relationships: the familiar form was used with family, close friends, children, and social inferiors, while the polite form conveyed deference or distance, and choosing the wrong form could be construed as a serious Ⓑ<u>insult</u>. Most countries combat smoking with taxes, warning labels, and bans on advertising, and these measures have curtailed smoking rates substantially, yet young people still take up the habit every year. In 1972 the psychologist Irving Janis introduced the term groupthink to describe a pattern he found in several calamitous decisions, including the abortive American invasion of Cuba at the Bay of Pigs in 1961. Mangrove forests flourish along tropical coastlines, where their gnarled roots rise out of salty, muddy water. For centuries many people regarded them as Ⓐ<u>worthless</u> swamps, and vast expanses were cleared for shrimp farms, hotels, and ports. Some psychologists claim that reading novels can render people more sympathetic toward others, but the evidence for this claim is still disputed. Ⓑ The novel became a popular literary form in eighteenth-century Europe, when printing grew cheaper and literacy spread. Ⓒ In several studies, people who read a short literary story performed marginally better on tests of recognizing emotions than those who read nonfiction or nothing at all. Ⓓ Other researchers, however, have struggled to replicate these effects, and some conjecture that people who are already empathetic simply opt to read more fiction. Dengue is a viral disease spread mainly by Aedes mosquitoes, and most infections cause either no symptoms or a fever that subsides within a week. ( Ⓐ ) A small fraction of cases, however, become severe, causing internal hemorrhaging and sometimes death. ( Ⓑ ) In 2024 the world recorded more than ten million cases of dengue, far more than in any preceding year, with Brazil and other Latin American countries grievously afflicted. ( Ⓒ ) Warmer temperatures allow the mosquitoes to thrive in regions that were once too cool for them, and torrential rains leave pools of stagnant water in which they proliferate. ( Ⓓ ) Cases have now been reported in parts of southern Europe, where the disease was once virtually unknown. Many accomplished people privately harbor the belief that they do not deserve their success. In 1978 the psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described this experience among high-achieving women, who attributed their achievements to luck, timing, or other people's erroneous judgments rather than to their own aptitude. Since then, the impostor phenomenon, as it came to be called, has been reported among men and women alike, from university students to senior executives. Those affected often toil extremely hard to evade being "found out," and each new success brings relief rather than assurance. Researchers underscore that it is not a mental illness but a common pattern of thinking, and that talking candidly about it with peers or mentors often reveals how prevalent it is.

A single bolt of lightning can heat the ambient air to about 30,000 kelvins, several times hotter than the surface of the sun. The air expands so abruptly that it generates a shock wave, which we hear as thunder. Because light travels far faster than sound, we see the flash almost instantaneously but hear the thunder later; counting the seconds between the two and dividing by three gives an approximate distance in kilometers. Contrary to a popular adage, lightning often strikes the same place more than once. Lofty structures are especially frequent targets: the Empire State Building in New York is struck around twenty times in a typical year. Most flashes, however, occur within or between clouds rather than between a cloud and the ground.

The Montessori method is an approach to early education built on children's freedom to choose their own activities. Maria Montessori, one of the first women to qualify as a physician in Italy, devised it while working with young children in an impoverished district of Rome in the early 1900s. She discerned that children learned best when they could choose their own activities from a meticulously prepared environment and work at their own pace. Montessori classrooms therefore contain child-sized furniture and specially designed materials, such as wooden letters and beads for counting, which children manipulate on their own. Teachers act as facilitators rather than lecturers, and children of different ages often share a classroom so that younger pupils can learn from older ones. Today thousands of schools around the world invoke her name, though not all of them adhere to her methods scrupulously.

Japan's rice price surge of 2024 and 2025 sparked a debate about farm policy. Because rice is central to Japanese meals and identity, the surge caused inordinate alarm. Officials at first avowed that total supplies were adequate. Several causes were Ⓑ<u>blaming</u>: a scorching summer in 2023 had blighted much of the crop, a burgeoning number of tourists bolstered demand at restaurants, and some households hoarded rice after a government warning about a possible major earthquake. Economists also pointed to a longer-term problem: for decades the state had paid farmers to curb production in order to keep prices stable, leaving the country with scant spare capacity. In 2025 officials took the rare step of releasing grain from the national emergency reserve, Ⓒ<u>which</u> is ordinarily kept for disasters and poor harvests. Prices abated somewhat, but the episode precipitated debate about an aging farm workforce, Ⓓ<u>whose</u> average age is close to seventy, and about whether policies designed for an era of surplus Ⓔ<u>remain</u> suitable today.

Smartphones and laptops have made it possible to work from almost anywhere, but they have also made it hard to stop working. The law applied first to medium and large businesses and was extended to small businesses a year later. Critics contend that such rules are too Ⓓ<u>rigid</u> for jobs that involve clients in distant time zones or genuine emergencies. Advocates retort that the laws do not ban after-hours contact; they simply protect workers who elect not to respond, and they encourage employers to Ⓔ<u>plan</u> work more judiciously.

More than two thousand years ago, Aristotle identified three means by which a speaker can Ⓐ<u>persuade</u> an audience. The first, ethos, hinges on the speaker's character: we are more disposed to believe people who seem erudite, honest, and well-intentioned. The second, pathos, works through the audience's emotions, Ⓑ<u>stirring</u> anger, pity, fear, or hope. The third, logos, appeals to reason through evidence and argument. A cogent speech, in his view, usually combines all three rather than relying on any one of them alone. Aristotle regarded logos as the heart of persuasion, but he did not think that logic alone was Ⓒ<u>insufficient</u>; he was pragmatic enough to recognize that audiences are rarely swayed by argument alone, and he treated emotional appeals as entirely legitimate when they fit the facts of the case. The framework has proved remarkably Ⓓ<u>durable</u>: modern advertisers rely on endorsements by reputable experts or celebrities, which borrow ethos, and on images of happy families, which aim at pathos. Political speechwriters interweave all three, teachers of rhetoric still use the three terms, and readers who learn to recognize them in action become appreciably harder to Ⓔ<u>manipulate</u>.

The idea of a universal basic income, a regular cash payment given to every citizen with no conditions attached, has attracted adherents from across the political spectrum. Advocates on the left see it as a way to alleviate poverty, while some on the right Ⓐ<u>condemn</u> it as a simpler replacement for convoluted welfare programs. To test the idea, Finland ran a two-year experiment beginning in 2017, in which two thousand unemployed people were selected at random to receive 560 euros a month, which they retained even if they found work. ____, under the ordinary system, taking a job could mean forfeiting benefits, which critics said Ⓑ<u>discouraged</u> people from accepting low-paid or temporary work. The results, published in full in 2020, were equivocal: recipients worked only marginally more days than a comparison group, a Ⓒ<u>modest</u> effect, but they described themselves as less stressed, healthier, and more trusting of institutions. Advocates lauded the experiment as a Ⓓ<u>success</u>; skeptics countered that it was too small and too short to show how a nationwide program would work, or how it could be Ⓔ<u>financed</u>. The debate, in short, is far from settled.

q:
밑줄 친 낱말과 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것을 고르시오.
Our <u>garrulous</u> tour guide filled every silence with anecdotes about local history, and by noon even the most inquisitive visitors were yearning for a few tranquil minutes.
garrulous 는 '말이 많은, 수다스러운'이라 voluble(말이 많은, 입심 좋은)과 가까워요. 침묵이 생길 때마다 이야기로 채웠다는 설명이 단서이고, taciturn(말수 적은)은 반대예요.

밑줄 친 낱말과 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것을 고르시오.
Known for being <u>fastidious</u> about detail, the editor returned every manuscript replete with notes on commas, spacing, and the spelling of peripheral characters' names.
fastidious 는 '아주 꼼꼼한, 까다로운'이라 scrupulous(빈틈없이 꼼꼼한)와 가까워요. 쉼표·띄어쓰기·조연 이름 철자까지 지적했다는 뒤 내용이 단서예요.

밑줄 친 낱말과 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것을 고르시오.
Officials conceded that the housing shortage had become an <u>intractable</u> problem, one that had withstood every reform attempted over the preceding two decades.
intractable 은 '다루기 힘든, 고질적인'이라 refractory(다루기 힘든, 고집 센)와 가까워요. 20년 동안 어떤 개혁에도 버텼다는 설명이 단서이고, tractable(다루기 쉬운)은 반대예요.

밑줄 친 낱말과 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것을 고르시오.
The student <u>surreptitiously</u> checked his phone under the desk, hoping that the professor, who was engrossed in writing on the board, would not notice.
surreptitiously 는 '몰래, 남의 눈을 피해'라 stealthily(살그머니)와 같은 뜻이에요. 책상 아래에서, 교수가 눈치채지 않기를 바랐다는 내용이 단서이고, ostensibly(겉보기에는)는 뜻이 달라요.

밑줄 친 낱말과 뜻이 가장 비슷한 것을 고르시오.
Many freelance translators live in a <u>precarious</u> financial situation, never certain whether next month's commissions will be enough to cover the rent.
precarious 는 '불안정한, 위태로운'이라 tenuous(불안정한, 위태롭게 버티는)와 가까워요. 다음 달 일감으로 월세를 낼 수 있을지 늘 확신하지 못한다는 설명이 단서예요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Because only twelve patients took part in the trial, the researchers described their conclusions as ____ and advocated larger studies before any alteration in treatment.
환자가 열두 명뿐이라 더 큰 연구를 요청했으니 결론은 '잠정적인(tentative)' 것이에요. conclusive(결정적인)는 정반대예요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
In many traditional households, younger members are expected to show ____, a respectful yielding to the judgment of their elders, by letting them speak first at the dinner table.
빈칸 바로 뒤에서 '어른의 판단에 공손히 따르는 것'이라고 풀어 주니 '존중, 경의(deference)'예요. 어른이 먼저 말하게 한다는 예도 같은 뜻이에요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Installing automatic sprinklers in every warehouse would largely ____ the need for the onerous overnight fire patrols that the company currently employs.
자동 스프링클러를 달면 부담스러운(onerous) 야간 순찰이 필요 없어지니 '(필요를) 없애다(obviate)'가 맞아요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Malaria remains ____ in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, where it is perpetually present among the inhabitants rather than arriving in occasional outbreaks.
가끔 터지는 것이 아니라 늘 주민 사이에 있다는 설명이 바로 '풍토성의(endemic)' 뜻이에요. sporadic(산발적인)은 반대예요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Thick walls of stone or earth do more than keep a house warm in winter. They also ____ the noise of traffic and neighbors, which is why old monasteries often feel remarkably tranquil even in the midst of bustling cities.
두꺼운 벽 덕분에 번화한 도시 한가운데서도 조용하다고 했으니 소음을 '약하게 하다(attenuate)'가 맞아요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
After three abortive attempts to persuade the committee, she began to sense the ____ of arguing any further. The members had evidently made up their minds long before the meeting began.
위원들이 회의 전에 이미 마음을 정했으니 더 따져 봐야 '소용없음(futility)'을 느낀 거예요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Some people have a stronger ____ for risk than others; they are quicker to gamble, invest in volatile stocks, or take up perilous sports. Studies of twins suggest that this tendency is partly hereditary, although upbringing also plays a role.
도박·변동 큰 주식·위험한 운동에 더 빨리 뛰어든다는 뒤 설명이 단서라 위험을 좋아하는 '성향(propensity)'이에요. aversion(싫어함)은 뒤 설명과 부딪쳐요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Companies rarely announce that they are firing workers. Instead, they speak of "rightsizing" or "streamlining operations," a ____ designed to make painful news sound mundane and almost innocuous.
해고를 '적정 규모화'처럼 부드럽게 바꿔 말하는 것은 '완곡어법(euphemism)'이에요. 아픈 소식을 평범하고 무해하게 들리게 한다는 뒤 설명도 같은 뜻이에요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
When people envision a bee, they usually imagine a teeming hive ruled by a queen. Yet the overwhelming majority of the world's roughly 20,000 bee species live quite differently. Most are ____: each female builds her own small nest, often a tunnel in the soil or a hollow plant stem, forages for pollen by herself, and lays her eggs without the help of any workers. Because they have no hive or stored honey to defend, these bees rarely sting, which makes them congenial neighbors for gardeners who want their fruit trees pollinated.
암컷 한 마리가 혼자 둥지를 짓고 꽃가루를 모으며 일벌 도움 없이 알을 낳는다고 했으니 '홀로 사는(solitary)'이 맞아요. 거의 쏘지 않는다고 했으니 belligerent(호전적인)도 아니에요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Parents who read to young children are often told that the stories themselves matter less than the conversation around them. When an adult pauses to ask what a character might do next, or links a picture to the child's own experience, the child must articulate his or her thoughts. Researchers call this dialogic reading, and studies suggest that it can substantially ____ a preschooler's vocabulary, especially when the sessions are brief, frequent, and playful rather than long and dutiful. The book, in other words, works best as an invitation to talk.
아이가 생각을 말로 옮겨야 하는 대화식 읽기는 어휘를 크게 '늘린다(augment)'는 흐름이에요. 책이 대화로 이끄는 초대장 구실을 한다는 마무리와도 맞아요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Lifeguards face a peculiar mental challenge. For hours at a time almost nothing happens, yet a swimmer in trouble may slip silently beneath the surface in less than a minute. Psychologists who study sustained attention have found that ____ declines sharply after only twenty or thirty minutes of monitoring an uneventful scene. For this reason, many pools rotate their guards among different stations at regular intervals, so that each person has a fresh vantage point before attention begins to wane.
지속적 주의(sustained attention)를 연구했고, 아무 일 없는 장면을 20~30분 지켜보면 급격히 떨어진다고 했으니 '경계심(vigilance)'이에요. 주의가 약해지기 전에 자리를 바꾼다는 마무리도 같은 뜻이에요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Why do adults who learned to ride a bicycle as children never forget how? Skills of this kind are stored in procedural memory, a system that operates largely below conscious awareness. Repetition gradually shifts control of a movement away from deliberate thought, so that a pianist no longer has to think about where each finger goes. Coaches therefore insist on correct technique from the outset: once a flawed movement has been practised thousands of times, it becomes deeply ____ and is notoriously hard to unlearn.
수천 번 연습한 잘못된 동작은 몸에 깊이 '배어 버려(ingrained)' 고치기 어렵다는 흐름이에요. 반복이 동작을 의식적 생각 밖으로 옮긴다는 앞 내용이 단서예요.

In the 1940s, the psychologist B. F. Skinner showed that animals learn quickly when a reward follows a particular action. A pigeon that receives grain only after pecking a certain key soon pecks it avidly. What matters, Skinner found, is that the reward is ____ on the behavior. When food arrived at fixed intervals regardless of what the birds did, some developed peculiar rituals, turning in circles or bobbing their heads, as if their actions had summoned the meal. Skinner called this "superstition" in the pigeon.
특정 행동을 한 뒤에만 먹이를 줄 때 빨리 배운다고 했으니 보상이 행동에 '달려 있어야(contingent on)' 해요. 행동과 상관없이 먹이를 주자 엉뚱한 의식이 생겼다는 대비가 단서예요.

빈칸에 넣기에 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
Why do people happily watch a favorite film for the tenth time, or reread a novel whose ending they already know? One might expect such experiences to be tedious, since nothing in them can surprise us. Researchers who study entertainment suggest the opposite: because the plot is ____, viewers are free to notice details they missed before, to savor the dialogue, and to enjoy a consoling sense of mastery. Familiar stories are especially popular in times of adversity, when the world outside feels volatile.
결말을 이미 아는 이야기라 줄거리가 '뻔히 예상되기(predictable)' 때문에 오히려 세부를 즐길 여유가 생긴다는 흐름이에요.

During the Second World War, military analysts studied bombers returning from missions and meticulously recorded where they had been hit by enemy fire. Bullet holes clustered on the wings and the body, while the engines showed relatively few. The evident conclusion was to add armor where the damage was most extensive. The statistician Abraham Wald is said to have identified the fallacy in this reasoning: the analysts were looking only at the planes that had made it back. Aircraft hit in the engines rarely returned at all, so the missing holes revealed where a plane was most vulnerable. The error, now called survivorship bias, appears whenever we study only the successes, such as renowned dropouts who became billionaires. To avoid it, one must ____.
add more armor wherever the damage seems most extensive
trust the obvious conclusion drawn from the available evidence
collect many more records from the planes that returned safely
consider the cases that failed and never appear in the data
rely on the judgment of experienced military analysts
돌아온 비행기만 보고 판단하면 엔진에 맞아 돌아오지 못한 비행기를 놓치게 돼요. 그래서 '생존 편향'을 피하려면 실패해 자료에 남지 않은 경우까지 따져 봐야 해요. '피해가 가장 커 보이는 곳에 장갑을 더한다'·'돌아온 비행기 기록을 더 모은다'는 바로 그 잘못된 추론이에요.

밑줄 친 Ⓐ~Ⓔ 가운데 어법에 맞지 않는 것을 고르시오.
In 1783 two brothers from a family of French paper makers, Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier, Ⓐ<u>astonished</u> spectators by launching a large balloon of paper and cloth filled with hot air. Later that year a sheep, a duck, and a rooster Ⓑ<u>were sent</u> aloft in a basket before the king at Versailles, a test meant to ascertain whether living creatures could survive at altitude. All three landed unscathed. Within weeks, two men Ⓒ<u>made</u> the first free flight by humans, drifting over Paris for about twenty-five minutes. The brothers mistakenly believed that a peculiar gas in the smoke Ⓓ<u>lifted</u> the balloon; in fact, it was simply the heated air, lighter than the cooler air around it, Ⓔ<u>what</u> carried them upward.
it was ~ that 강조 구문이라 강조한 말(the heated air) 뒤에는 that 이 와야 해요. what 은 선행사를 품은 관계대명사라 이 자리에 쓸 수 없어요.

In 1921 the Swiss psychiatrist Hermann Rorschach published a test Ⓐ<u>that</u> asked patients to describe what they saw in ten symmetrical inkblots. The images, Ⓑ<u>printed</u> on stiff cards, were meant to reveal how a person organizes what he or she perceives. Rorschach died the following year, but the test became renowned, and for decades it was used in clinics and even in courtrooms. To many researchers this popularity was Ⓒ<u>puzzled</u>, since studies consistently found that different examiners scored the same answers in different ways. The meaning of a response, critics argued, Ⓓ<u>depends</u> too heavily on the examiner's own judgment. Modern scoring systems have tried Ⓔ<u>to address</u> these concerns, but the test remains contentious.
인기가 연구자들을 '어리둥절하게 만든' 것이니 능동의 puzzling 이 맞아요. puzzled 는 어리둥절함을 느끼는 사람에게 써요.

밑줄 친 Ⓐ~Ⓔ 가운데 어법에 맞지 않는 것을 고르시오.
Paper was invented in China, and for centuries the technique of making it Ⓐ<u>remained</u> largely unknown elsewhere. According to a popular account, Chinese papermakers Ⓑ<u>captured</u> at a battle in Central Asia in 751 taught their craft to their captors, and paper mills soon appeared in Samarkand and Baghdad. Historians now surmise that the knowledge diffused more gradually, but there is no doubt that paper Ⓒ<u>transformed</u> the Islamic world, where it was used for books, maps, and government records. Ⓓ<u>Despite</u> parchment was more durable, paper was far cheaper to produce, and it allowed scholars Ⓔ<u>to copy</u> texts in great numbers.
despite 는 전치사라 뒤에 주어·동사가 갖춰진 절(parchment was more durable)을 받을 수 없어요. 접속사 Although 가 와야 해요.

밑줄 친 Ⓐ~Ⓔ 가운데 어법에 맞지 않는 것을 고르시오.
When the Eiffel Tower was built for the Paris World's Fair of 1889, it was Ⓐ<u>intended</u> to stand for only twenty years. Even before construction was finished, a petition signed by dozens of prominent artists and writers Ⓑ<u>were</u> published in a newspaper, denouncing the tower as useless and grotesque. Gustave Eiffel defended the structure, Ⓒ<u>arguing</u> that its engineering had a beauty of its own. As the end of its permit approached, the tower was saved largely by its usefulness: it served as a platform for experiments with radio, which made it Ⓓ<u>valuable</u> to the military. Today it is one of the most visited monuments in the world, and few Parisians can imagine their skyline Ⓔ<u>without</u> it.
주어의 중심은 a petition(청원서 하나)이라 단수예요. 사이에 든 signed by dozens of ~ writers 에 끌리지 말고 was published 로 받아야 해요.

남의 하품을 보거나 듣거나 읽기만 해도 하품이 나온다고 했으니 하품은 암시에 아주 '잘 넘어가는(susceptible)' 행동이에요. '잘 버티는(resistant)'은 콜론 뒤 설명과 반대예요.
밑줄 친 Ⓐ~Ⓔ 가운데 글의 흐름에 어울리지 않는 낱말을 고르시오.
물 위의 얼음이 아래 물의 열이 빠져나가는 것을 늦춘다고 했으니 열을 막는 '단열재(insulator)' 구실이에요. 열을 잘 전하는 '전도체(conductor)'는 흐름과 반대예요.
Ⓐ~Ⓔ 가운데 글의 흐름과 관계없는 문장을 고르시오.
글은 가르치려고 공부하거나 실제로 설명해 보면 더 잘 배운다는 '가르치며 배우기(프로테제 효과)' 내용이에요. 대학이 강의를 녹화해 올린다는 Ⓓ 문장은 이 흐름과 관계없어요.

글의 흐름으로 보아 다음 문장이 들어가기에 가장 알맞은 곳을 고르시오.
Many scientists worry that this crowding is bringing the world closer to a danger first described almost half a century ago, in which the debris problem would begin to feed on itself.
주어진 문장의 this crowding(이 북적임)은 바로 앞 '회사들이 위성 수천 기를 쏘아 올렸다'를 가리키고, '반세기 전에 처음 말한 위험'은 바로 뒤 1978년 케슬러의 경고로 풀려요. 그래서 Ⓓ 자리가 맞아요.
Ⓐ, Ⓑ, Ⓒ 의 괄호 안에서 문맥에 맞는 낱말끼리 짝지은 것을 고르시오.
아이스킬로스에서 길던 합창이 에우리피데스에 와서 줄거리와 느슨해졌으니 역할은 '줄었고(diminished)', 배우 수는 하나에서 셋으로 '늘었어요(increased)'. 합창을 빼면 작가가 만든 형식을 '훼손한다(distorts)'가 맞아요.
글의 주제로 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.
why a combined print and online subscription seemed like a bargain
the pricing of print and online magazine subscriptions
how removing unpopular options leads people to pay more
the importance of candor in modern advertising campaigns
how an unattractive extra option can steer people's choices
아무도 고르지 않는 선택지가 끼어 있기만 해도 다른 선택지가 싸 보여 사람들의 선택이 바뀐다는 '미끼 효과'를 설명하는 글이에요. 잡지 구독 이야기는 예시 하나일 뿐이고, 인쇄판만 있는 선택지를 빼자 오히려 싼 온라인판을 더 골랐으니 '빼면 돈을 더 쓴다'는 글과 반대예요.
글의 내용과 맞지 않는 것을 고르시오.
덫의 안쪽에는 작은 감지 털이 늘어서 있다.
감지 털을 한 번만 건드려도 덫이 바로 닫힌다.
이 방식 덕분에 빗방울에 쓸데없이 힘을 쓰지 않는다.
벌레를 다 흡수하는 데 일주일 넘게 걸리기도 한다.
야생에서는 미국의 좁은 습지 지역에서만 자란다.
털 하나를 한 번 건드리면 아무 일도 없고, 20초 안에 두 번째로 건드려야 닫힌다고 했어요. 한 번만 건드려도 닫힌다는 문장이 글과 맞지 않아요.
